query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of aluminum into the base high‐entropy alloy will improve mechanical durability, reduce room‐temperature creep rates, and enhance corrosion resistance by promoting a strengthened microstructure and stable, protective surface oxides.
generation.material_initial_state: An aerospace fastener high‐entropy alloy in its baseline composition (e.g., a CoCrFeNi- or FeCrNi-based HEA with an FCC-dominated structure and limited inherent creep resistance and moderate corrosion resistance).
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by adding a modest, optimized molar fraction of aluminum (around 0.7 molar ratio based on prior studies) into the base HEA composition.
generation.conditions: Performance evaluated under room-temperature mechanical testing (tensile and nanoindentation creep tests) and under corrosion conditions such as exposure to a neutral chloride environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) typical of aerospace service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A microstructure in which aluminum addition promotes a transition from a primarily FCC structure to a dual-phase (FCC+BCC) or dominantly BCC solid solution with enhanced lattice distortion and a refined grain structure, along with the in situ formation of a stable alumina (Al2O3) passivation layer at the surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, owing to its large atomic radius and high oxide-forming tendency, increases solid-solution strengthening and potentially triggers the formation of hard BCC phases that resist dislocation creep at room temperature. Concurrently, its oxidation during service produces a protective Al2O3 film that impedes corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated baseline, the modified alloy is expected to exhibit higher yield strength and lower creep strain rate (indicating enhanced room-temperature creep resistance) as well as improved corrosion parameters (e.g., lower corrosion current density) due to the formation of a robust passivation film.
generation.baseline: The untreated HEA fastener alloy with an unmodified composition possessing moderate mechanical durability, creep behavior, and corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: The benefits of the Al addition are expected to hold for aerospace fastener components operating under ambient (room temperature) mechanical loads and in moderately corrosive environments; however, excessively high Al levels or exposure to extreme service conditions could lead to unwanted phase formation or embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal aluminum content and its effects may vary with the specific base alloy composition and processing history. There is some uncertainty regarding the exact phase evolution and long-term stability of the protective oxide layer under cyclic aerospace conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline HEA (e.g., CoCrFeNi-based alloy) and another set with an optimized aluminum addition (around 0.7 mol fraction). Process both sets identically (e.g., casting, hot rolling, and controlled heat treatment to homogenize the microstructure). Subject specimens to room-temperature tensile and nanoindentation creep tests and expose them to a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution in a salt spray chamber for a defined duration.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and elongation at room temperature
Creep strain rate measured via nanoindentation at ambient temperature
Electrochemical corrosion tests (potentiodynamic polarization to determine corrosion current density and passivation behavior)
Microstructural characterization (XRD, SEM, EBSD) to identify phase constitution and grain size
Surface analysis (XPS) to confirm formation and stability of the Al2O3 passivation layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-added samples do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., at least a measurable increase in yield strength, a lower creep strain rate, and improved corrosion resistance parameters) compared to the baseline, or if the modified alloy develops deleterious phases or unstable oxide films under the test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In the present investigation, Ti-V-Nb-Ta samples were subjected to thermal aging for various durations at 700°C. The microstructure and mechanical properties of Ti-V-Nb-Ta before and after thermal aging were revealed by a combination of state-of-the-art microstructural characterization and nanoindentation techniques. Results indicate that impurity interstitials at the trace levels within the solid solution encourage the formation of α-Ti precipitates in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy when aged at high temperature, which undermines the effects of interstitial solid solution strengthening and leads to softening.

Structural components used in high-temperature environments often fail due to high-temperature creep. Traditional creep tests, such as uniaxial tensile or compression tests, often require large sample sizes and long testing periods, which has limited the research on the creep properties of RHEAs. To overcome these limitations, the use of nanoindentation techniques for studying creep behavior offers an effective alternative. Nanoindentation is applying a small indentation load on the surface of the material to measure its mechanical properties, allowing for the assessment of creep properties at a very small scale. The advantages of this technique include the small size of samples required and short experimental periods. Existing research indicates that adding Al to CoCrFeNiCu alloys results in a phase transformation from FCC to BCC structures. Although this addition reduces the ductility of the alloy, it effectively enhances its creep resistance at the nanoscale [].
